title: Rescuers blocked from a fire. A child killed on the way to school. Miles-long trains are upending US lives
summary:
Communities say big railroad companies won’t act and that lawmakers moving too slowly to address a major problem

The drive from the Lockland fire station to a house fire on Patterson Avenue…

blocks.text: The drive from the Lockland fire station to a house fire on Patterson Avenue should have taken no more than 45 seconds.

But East Wyoming Avenue and Davis Street were both blocked: a Norfolk Southern train was stopped across several streets – the fire engine had to turn around and take a detour via a nearby highway. By the time firefighters snaked through the highway traffic and reached the fire last month, seven minutes after the call came in, 89-year-old Marian Haefner was dead in her own home.
“We lost a house here about five years ago, on Central Avenue which is directly on the other side of the tracks. Same thing, couldn’t get to it,” says Mark Mason, Lockland’s mayor.
“I’ve been mayor of Lockland for nine years. Frankly, [Norfolk Southern] don’t give a crap. If they did, they would do something about it.”

From his office in a century-old building in Lockland, a small community north of Cincinnati, Mason reels off a list of complaints about train crossing blockages he’s been fielding: People threatened with dismissal because they are constantly late to work. Parents paying extra to daycares because they’re late picking up their children. College students who have had to drop out of a class because they can’t get to campus on time.

Lockland is several miles south of the Sharonville intermodal terminal, a link of the Heartland Corridor that links an Atlantic seaport in Norfolk, Virginia, with Chicago. It is from this terminal that Norfolk Southern trains are moved on to the tracks across Lockland streets, sometimes for up to 23 hours, to make room for other trains to be connected, say local officials.

“I’ve had it. It’s 2026 – trains should not be affecting people’s lives like this, much less putting them in danger. It’s an easy fix – quit pulling out trains if they can’t move forward [but train companies] are a powerful entity,” Mason says.
Rail companies own most tracks and lines in the US. Local and state authorities have scant ability to regulate.
Lockland is far from alone in dealing with Norfolk Southern, a $73bn public company with a long line of environmental and other charges against it.
Similar rail crossing incidents have been happening in Cleveland, Chicago, Houston and beyond.

In Hammond, Indiana a 2023 Pro Publica investigation found children regularly having to climb through cars to get to and from school. Local administrators say Norfolk Southern backed out of building a pedestrian overpass.

Over the past 12 months there have been more than 34,000 public reports of rail crossing blockages, according to the Federal Railroad Administration, a sharp increase from more than 25,000 reports over the previous 12 months. Texas alone made up almost 10,000 of those, with Ohio seeing the third-highest number of reports in that time.

In almost a quarter of those incidents, pedestrians crawling on, over or between rail cars were reported. In nearly 22%, first responders were unable to cross the tracks. Numerous other reports found students at the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa having to climb through stopped cars to get to campus.
In 2023, Houston reported 5,610 reports of blocked rail crossings, with the city’s East End reporting the highest number of complaints in the country, according to local reports.
Last December, Sylvia Garcia, a Texas congresswoman whose district includes the East End, reintroduced a bill prohibiting trains from blocking rail crossings for more than 10 minutes.

“We tragically lost 15-year-old Sergio Rodriguez, who was killed by an oncoming train while trying to get to Milby high school. No child should have to risk their life getting to school, and no family should have to worry about a blocked train delaying emergency care. Our communities deserve better,” she says.

“Republicans have allowed this legislation to languish in committee while powerful railroad companies continue putting their bottom lines ahead of the safety of our communities. These companies have spent years making promises while our families continue paying the price.”

Ohioans have had a troubled relationship with Norfolk Southern in recent years. In February 2023, a failed wheel bearing caused a train derailment and catastrophic chemical fire in East Palestine. The company settledwith the justice department and Environmental Protection Agency for more than $310m.

Last July, 19 rail cars carried on a Norfolk Southern train, including one containing hydrochloric acid, derailed in Bucyrus, Ohio, forcing emergency services to establish a one-mile evacuation zone and driving residents from their homes.
The Atlanta-headquartered company is in the midst of a merger attempt with Union Pacific, another freight rail behemoth and the owner of the train that killed Sergio Rodriguez in Houston.

JD Vance, Vice-president and Ohio native, has pushed for the passing of the Railway Safety Act, a bipartisan senate bill that calls for having two-person crews on board to operate a train. But rail companies have staunchly opposed the proposal, arguing one person is sufficient. Railroad lobbyists, which number in the hundreds, are among the most powerful and well-financed in Washington.
For its part, Norfolk Southern says changes it made to scheduling in Hammond, Indiana, has led to a 50% reduction in blocked crossing calls from residents.

“Norfolk Southern (NS) continues working with local officials to reduce the impact of blocked crossings, particularly for emergency responders. Those efforts include discussions around crossing-detection technology that could provide real-time visibility when crossings are occupied,” says a Norfolk Southern spokesperson.
“NS is making infrastructure investments in the [Lockland] area intended to help reduce congestion and minimize crossing impacts while maintaining safe operations.”
The spokesperson says the company is taking part in the Cincinnati Rail Congestion Mitigation Plan, “focused on improving rail fluidity and addressing blocked-crossing concerns across the corridor.”

There are no federal limits on maximum freight train lengths, with some recorded as being three miles in length. Others have argued that deregulation of the sector by the Trump administration has made matters worse for communities.

In August, Sean Duffy, transportation secretary, appeared in Cincinnati to announce funding for a swathe of national rail projects, including a proposed $40m grant to close two crossings and build a new bridge in nearby Fairfield, Ohio.
“The tragedy in Lockland is a reminder that the safest crossing is no crossing at all,” says Alex Murglin of the Federal Railroad Administration.

“Events like [the death of Marian Haefner] are why Secretary Duffy recently announced $1.24bn in grants to eliminate key crossings in 37 states and why FRA continues to work closely with railroads and local municipalities to reduce the occurrence of blockages at crossings.”
Still, for Lockland residents the threat of blocked streets isn’t going away anytime soon.
Dozens of homes on the east side are hemmed in by an interstate highway and creek to the east, and the Norfolk Southern rail line to the west.

Scott Fritsch’s Mueller Roofing Distributors has been operating in Lockland since 1875 and is the kind of local business where customers are greeted with free hotdogs inside the main door. But with some of his premises on either side of the Norfolk Southern railway, crossing blockages have been a nightmare for business.
“They can be stopped across the tracks for hours at times. You can’t get back and forth,” he says.
“They say they’ll look into it but it’s not getting any better. It’s been a constant battle for customers and our trucks not being able to get where they need to go.”

Nearby Cincinnati is one of the busiest rail hubs in the midwest, connecting industrial northern cities such as Chicago with freight destined for overseas markets via the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. CSX, which operates about 20,000 miles of track mostly in the eastern US and Canada, has a huge rail yard several miles south of Lockland that handles about 3,200 train cars at any one time.
Mason says Norfolk Southern representatives have been in touch following the death of Marian Haefner, but he hasn’t been impressed by their approach.
“They couldn’t make [a meeting in] November work, so that tells me the sort of urgency that Norfolk Southern feels about this,” he says.
“Lockland’s school is right here – it’s within a stone’s throw of the tracks, so you’ve got an unmanned train with all these chemical cars. Again, they don’t care.”
